summary: Enter a sky position , an object name, or Right Ascension and declination and Nejma finds every SPHEREx spectral image that covers it, stacks the images taken during each visit, and plays the visits back like a short video, so that anything that moved or changed in the infrared sky stands out.
details:
What it does and how it works:
Nejma is a public-facing, time-domain viewer built for NASA's SPHEREx mission. A user enters any sky position (name, RA/Dec, or a deep link to a test target), and Nejma queries the IRSA archive to find every SPHEREx spectral image covering that coordinate. Because SPHEREx visits the same regions roughly every six months, Nejma stacks these observations onto a common north-up grid and a consistent brightness scale, then plays them back as a time-lapse video. The interface includes a Blink/Difference mode where subtracting two visits reveals moving objects (half-black/half-white artifacts) or variable sources (full-frame flux changes).

Additionally, because each SPHEREx image contains spectral information, Nejma extracts a spectrum (0.75–5.0 µm) and a light curve directly from the stacked frames without requiring a separate spectroscopic pipeline.

We also integrated contextual overlays: Gaia DR3 proper-motion predictions for the visit date, contamination/saturation flags, and Aladin Lite cross-matches (2MASS, WISE, DSS) to validate the infrared detections.

Benefits and Intended Impact:
SPHEREx is producing an unprecedented all-sky spectral survey, but the raw data products are optimized for static cataloging. Nejma lowers the barrier for time-domain science and public engagement by making the mission's cadence and spectral coverage immediately intuitive. For researchers, it provides a rapid visual triage tool to identify variable or moving infrared sources (e.g., brown dwarfs like WISE 0855, or young stars like RW Aurigae) before committing to expensive spectroscopic follow-up. For the public and citizen scientists, it transforms a massive NASA dataset into an accessible, interactive "find the moving object" experience, directly supporting the Space Apps goal of making space data accessible.

Tools and Technologies:

  • Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA SPHEREx Quick Release (QR2/QR3) Spectral Images via the SIA2 protocol and cloud access.
  • Backend: Python (FastAPI, Uvicorn) for the live-query service; Astroquery and PyVO for VO-compliant IRSA queries; NumPy/AstroPy for WCS alignment and reprojection.
  • Frontend: JavaScript (Static viewer in docs/), Aladin Lite for contextual sky overlays.
  • Deployment: Vercel (static frontend + serverless Python API).
  • AI Use: Super Intelligence (LLMs) was used to accelerate boilerplate code generation (FastAPI routing, JS UI handlers) and to assist in drafting the WCS reprojection logic documentation. All scientific logic and data handling were validated by the team.
